facts.statement: The only known species, Qiupanykus zhangi, was named in honor of Shuancheng Zhang, who helped find the fossils.
facts.quote: The type and only species is Q. zhangi, named for Shuancheng Zhang, who assisted in finding the fossils of Qiupanykus.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in the Tantou Basin within Luanchuan County, Henan Province, China.
facts.quote: The Qiupa Formation is located in the Tantou Basin which is in Luanchuan County of the Henan province in China.

facts.statement: The Qiupa Formation dates to the end of the Maastrichtian stage, the final stage of the Mesozoic Era.
facts.quote: More specific analyses have suggested that the formation dates to the end of the Maastrichtian stage, which was the final stage of the Mesozoic Era.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, designated 41HIII-0101, is housed at the Henan Geological Museum in Zhengzhou.
facts.quote: The holotype, and only specimen of what would later be named Qiupanykus was prepared and stored at the Henan Geological Museum in Zhengzhou after being excavated and was given the designation 41HIII-0101.

facts.statement: The species was formally described in 2018 by a team led by Lü Junchang in the journal of the Chinese Geological Survey.
facts.quote: A full description was published in 2018 by Lü Junchang, Li Xu, Chang Huali, Jia Songhai, Zhang Jiming, Gao Diansong, Zhang Yiyang, Zhang Chengjun, and Ding Fang in the journal of the Chinese Geological Survey.

facts.statement: The femur measured approximately 74.2 mm, the tibia 98.6 mm, and the longest metatarsal 75.4 mm.
facts.quote: The femur was about 74.2 mm long, the tibia was about 98.6 mm long, and the longest metatarsal was about 75.4 mm.

facts.statement: The fully extended leg length was estimated to be about 24.8 cm.
facts.quote: This would give the leg, if fully extended, a total length of only about 24.8 cm.

facts.statement: Based on isometric scaling, the estimated body mass was 0.52 kg.
facts.quote: Lü and colleagues also used the dimensions of the femur to estimate an in-life mass of 0.52 kg based on isometric scaling methods.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies estimated the mass to be 0.58 kg.
facts.quote: Subsequent authors studying the evolution of miniaturization in alvarezsaurids gave a mass estimate of only 0.58 kg for Qiupanykus.

facts.statement: Another study suggested a possible mass range of 0.27 to 0.91 kg.
facts.quote: Another publication suggested a range of 0.27-0.91 kg for possible masses.

facts.statement: The holotype is a poorly preserved postcranial skeleton containing elements from all body regions.
facts.quote: The holotype of Qiupanykus consists of a relatively poorly-preserved postcranial skeleton that includes elements from all areas of the body.

facts.statement: The skeleton includes cervical, sacral, and caudal vertebrae, parts of the pelvis, an articulated right hindlimb, foot digits, and three pedal claws.
facts.quote: The elements present include four disarticulated cervical vertebrae, six sacral vertebrae, twenty-five caudal vertebrae with an associated chevron, part of the right ilium and ischium, part of the pubis, an articulated right hindlimb (including the femur, fibula, tibia, astragalus, calcaneum, and all three metatarsals), two digits of the foot, and three associated pedal claws.

facts.statement: The skeleton was found associated with eggshell fragments assigned to the ootaxon Arriagadoolithus.
facts.quote: Notably, the skeleton was also found in association with several fragments of eggshells which have been assigned to the ootaxon Arriagadoolithus.

facts.statement: Qiupanykus is distinguished by a strong sacral keel, midline caudal transverse processes, a reduced pubic peduncle, a large tibial crest, fused sacral-caudal vertebrae, and small pneumatic foramina on caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The presence of these features allowed Lü and colleagues to distinguish Qiupanykus from all other alvarezsaurs by the following combination of traits: a strong keel on the underside of the sacral vertebrae, transverse processes positioned on the midline of the centra of the caudal vertebrae at the base of the tail, a reduced knob-like pubic peduncle on the ilium, a large quadrangular crest on the tibia, the two vertebrae at the base of the tail being functionally part of the sacrum, and the presence of a small pneumatic foramen on each of the caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: The femur-to-tibia ratio and arctometatarsus suggest Qiupanykus was a capable runner.
facts.quote: Additionally, the ratio of the length of the femur to the tibia and the presence of an arctometatarsus suggest that Qiupanykus, like other alvarezsaurs, would have been a capable runner.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Qiupanykus at the base of Parvicursorinae in a polytomy with several other taxa.
facts.quote: Their strict consensus tree recovered Qiupanykus at the base of Parvicursorinae in a polytomy with Albertonykus, Linhenykus, Xixianykus, the specimen YPM 1049 ("Ornithomimus minutus"), and a clade containing the rest of the derived parvicursorines.

facts.statement: Although not formally assigned to Parvicursorinae in its description, its phylogenetic position makes it a member of that clade.
facts.quote: Although not formally assigned to the clade Parvicursorinae in the description, this position would make it a member of Parvicursorinae sensu Xu et al. (2013).

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Meso, Pol, and Makovicky reaffirmed Qiupanykus as a member of Parvicursorinae.
facts.quote: In 2024, a team of authors led by Jorge Gustavo Meso and including the theropod researchers Diego Pol and Peter Makovicky published a study examining the evolutionary history of Alvarezsauria.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Qiupanykus reflects a miniaturization event in alvarezsaurian evolution during the early-to-middle Cenomanian.
facts.quote: They found Qiupanykus as a member of Parvicursorinae and suggested that its appearance is reflective of a "miniaturization event" within alvarezsaurian evolution that occurred during the early-to-middle Cenomanian.

facts.statement: Multiple authors suggest the associated egg ootaxon Arriagadoolithus may have been laid by Qiupanykus.
facts.quote: The ootaxon found in association with Qiupanykus, given the name Arriagadoolithus, has been suggested by multiple authors to possibly have been laid by Qiupanykus, even if not necessarily the individual which was preserved.

facts.statement: The egg was likely too massive for the holotype individual to have laid, suggesting it belonged to a larger parent.
facts.quote: Lü and colleagues estimated that in life, the egg would have been more massive than the holotype, making it unlikely that the holotype individual was the egg's parent.

facts.statement: Modern kiwis lay eggs that are 20% of the mother's mass, illustrating how miniaturization can lead to disproportionately large eggs.
facts.quote: The kiwi bird is the foremost example of this phenomenon as females famously lay a single giant egg (20% the mass of the mother) in every clutch.

facts.statement: No skull remains are known, so feeding habits cannot be directly inferred from skull anatomy.
facts.quote: No remains of the skull of Qiupanykus are known, so no direct observations about its possible feeding habits based on the anatomy of its skull can be inferred.

facts.statement: The unique hand morphology suggests alvarezsaurids may have specialized in feeding on colonial insects like ants.
facts.quote: These simultaneous developments, coupled with the unique morphology of alvarezsaurid hands, has been used to suggest that they may have been specialized to feed on colonial insects like ants.

facts.statement: The eggshells resemble those attributed to oviraptorosaurs found elsewhere in the Qiupa Formation.
facts.quote: These eggshells, later given the name Arriagadoolithus, closely resemble elongatoolithid eggs found at Luanchuan County elsewhere in the Qiupa Formation that are attributed to oviraptorosaurs.

facts.statement: Juvenile oviraptorosaur fossils found near Qiupanykus support the link between the eggs and oviraptorosaurs.
facts.quote: This is supported by the discovery of fossils from juvenile oviraptorosaurs in the vicinity of Qiupanykus.

facts.statement: Scaling estimates place the egg mass at about 1136 g, which exceeds the estimated mass of the holotype.
facts.quote: Also of note, the scaling methods used to estimate the full size of these eggshells, yielded a mass of about 1136 g, which is larger than the estimated mass of the holotype of Qiupanykus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the large hand claws were used to break eggshells for feeding.
facts.quote: They also suggested that the large hand claws on their short arms would have assisted in breaking eggshells to feed.

facts.statement: Some subsequent authors argue that the egg could still have belonged to Qiupanykus despite the size discrepancy.
facts.quote: Subsequent authors have suggested that it should not be ruled out that the egg belonged to Qiupanykus.

facts.statement: Qiupanykus fossils were found in strata that correspond to the K-T boundary and the beginning of the Cenozoic era.
facts.quote: Section C, in which Qiupanykus was found, is the youngest of these sections, and this section preserves strata that correspond exactly to the K-T boundary and the beginning of the Cenozoic.

facts.statement: The sedimentary layer containing Qiupanykus was deposited by a braided river delta.
facts.quote: This sedimentary layer would have been deposited by a braided river delta that created the depositional environment necessary for fossils to form.

facts.statement: The area where Qiupanykus lived is interpreted as having been a coastal environment at the end of the Cretaceous Period.
facts.quote: This area is also interpreted as having been part of a coastal environment during the end of the Cretaceous Period.

facts.statement: Qiupanykus lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Qiupanykus belongs to the parent group Alvarezsauroidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Alvarezsauroidea

facts.statement: Qiupanykus is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Qiupanykus is Qiupanykus zhangi.
facts.quote: Type species: Qiupanykus zhangi

facts.statement: More complete fossil remains are known from small theropods in this area than from large dinosaurs.
facts.quote: More complete remains are known from small theropods.

facts.statement: The environment included turtles, lizards like Tianyusaurus, small mammals, and the uniquely edentulous enantiornithine Yuornis.
facts.quote: These would have included turtles, lizards (such as the genus Tianyusaurus), small mammals, and uniquely an edentulous enantiornithine Yuornis.
